parts: Please read /papers/investigations-6/05_arithmetic_gap_continuation/03_explicit_zero_gap_transport/brainstorm/notes/08_EZ_WHY_THE_INVERSE_HAS_A_CUTOFF_20261120.md. I'd like to get better intuition for what the formulas we are developing are accomplishing and how they relate to the broader ideas within the program. Can you start by explaining more clearly why the approximations for the zeros get better with higher height but the formulas are centering around K(T) which is the height at which the approximation starts failing? I still don't understand what is going on exactly. You can refer to the previous conversation as well for more context.
I’ll read the note and the surrounding discussion, then explain how improving accuracy at higher zeros fits with the cutoff \(K(T)\).

The key distinction is that the note uses two different approximations. The one that improves as you move higher is the fixed-time high-zero formula. \(K(T)\) belongs to the large-heat-time inverse formula, and marks the end of a proved range—not a known point of failure. I’m checking the earlier discussion so I can make that distinction concrete.

The formula is actually built around zero height; \(K(T)\) is added afterward by the error analysis. The useful intuition is cancellation: higher heat time concentrates the source, making its average look like a simple cosine. Higher height makes that same average cancel more strongly, so it needs a different approximation. That explains why the two formulas improve in different directions.

**The formulas are centered at zero height. \(K(T)\) is introduced afterward to describe how far their present proof reaches.** It is a number of zeros, not a height, and it does not identify where the approximation starts failing.

The deeper issue is that there are **two different ways the same function becomes simpler**. The earlier discussion did not make their mechanisms distinct enough.

Here \(T\) is heat time, \(x\) is height, and \(k\) labels a zero. Think of fixing \(T\) as taking a snapshot of the entire infinite sequence of zeros. Increasing \(x\) moves along that snapshot. Increasing \(T\) changes the snapshot itself.

| What increases? | What becomes simpler? | Which formula uses it? |
|---|---|---|
| Heat time \(T\) | The source becomes concentrated and approximately Gaussian | Our inverse series \(Y\) |
| Height \(x\), at fixed positive time | The far-tail field approaches an explicit oscillatory expression | The high-zero formula |

To see what our series accomplishes, start with
\[
\frac{H_T(x)}{H_T(0)}=\mathbb E_T\cos(xU).
\]
This says: average the waves \(\cos(xu)\), weighting each \(u\) by the heated source.

Imagine first that all the source mass sits at one point \(a\). Then the average is exactly \(\cos(ax)\), and its zeros are
\[
x_k=\frac{(k-\tfrac12)\pi}{a}.
\]
They are equally spaced. There is nothing to approximate.

At large heat time, the actual source resembles a narrow mound around \(a\). Its width damps the average, and its asymmetry shifts the crossings. In the Gaussian approximation, the picture is
\[
\frac{H_T(x)}{H_T(0)}
\approx
e^{-\sigma_T^2x^2/2}
\cos\!\bigl(ax+\text{phase corrections}\bigr),
\]
where \(\sigma_T\) is the source’s width. **Our inverse series translates those phase corrections into corrections to the zero positions.** The cubic resummation incorporates the first asymmetric correction repeatedly. This is the structural content of the formula: source shape determines how the zeros depart from equal spacing. [Inverse construction]( /Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/05_arithmetic_gap_continuation/03_explicit_zero_gap_transport/manuscript/anchors.tex)

Now consider what happens when you increase height while keeping that mound fixed.

Two nearby source points separated by \(\sigma_T\) contribute waves whose angles differ by about
\[
x\sigma_T.
\]
As \(x\) grows, their contributions cancel more strongly. The Gaussian envelope \(e^{-\sigma_T^2x^2/2}\) becomes small.

**Knowing the source accurately does not automatically mean knowing its tiny, heavily cancelled average accurately.** An error that is small compared with the source can be large compared with the surviving oscillation. To locate its zeros, we must control the error relative to that oscillation.

That is what limits this particular approximation as height increases.

Increasing heat time helps in the opposite way: the source narrows, and its Gaussian approximation improves. Consequently, we can tolerate larger heights before the cancellation overwhelms our error bound.

The scale of \(K(T)\) comes from balancing these effects. The width is approximately \(1/\sqrt{\kappa}\). The proof’s relative-error estimate contains a factor of the form
\[
\kappa^{-1}(1+r^6)e^{r^2/2},
\]
where \(r\) measures height in units of \(\sqrt{\kappa}\). The factor \(\kappa^{-1}\) improves with heat time; the exponential grows as the height range expands. Choosing \(r\) proportional to \(\sqrt{\log\kappa}\) lets the improving source estimate win. Leaving additional room for inversion and adjacent-gap estimates gives
\[
K(T)=\left\lfloor
\frac{a\sqrt{\kappa\log\kappa}}{8\pi}+\frac12
\right\rfloor.
\]
Thus \(K(T)\) measures **how many consecutive zeros this argument controls simultaneously**. Its particular boundary reflects the proof’s margins. [Window derivation]( /Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/05_arithmetic_gap_continuation/03_explicit_zero_gap_transport/notes/11_EZ_GROWING_INVERSE_WINDOW_20261120.md)

The high-zero formula handles cancellation differently. For fixed \(0<t\le1/2\), the published description has the form
\[
H_t(x)=2A_t(x)\bigl(\cos\phi_t(x)+\varepsilon_t(x)\bigr),
\qquad \varepsilon_t(x)\to0.
\]
Here the error is already controlled **relative to the oscillatory amplitude** \(A_t(x)\). Positive heat increasingly suppresses the remaining arithmetic terms as height grows. The zeros therefore approach the crossings of this different phase, even in units of their local spacing. [Polymath, §9](https://arxiv.org/html/1904.12438v2#S9)

So “the approximation improves higher up” refers to that far-tail description. It does not say that the approximation obtained from the narrow source near its mean improves higher up. Both describe the same function, but they organize its cancellations differently.

There is also a distinction between the **full inverse** and its approximations. The full series \(Y\) is locally exact. However, its phase must still label successive zeros correctly. At fixed time, the half-line transform eventually crosses the same imaginary-axis direction repeatedly; its angle no longer counts zeros by successive half-turns. Resummation therefore needs a way to handle that change of phase description. \(K(T)\) does not locate that change. [Phase limitation]( /Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/05_arithmetic_gap_continuation/03_explicit_zero_gap_transport/notes/04_EZ_HALF_LINE_PHASE_OBSTRUCTION_20261120.md)

For the broader program, the value of the inverse formula is that one description of the source supplies a whole counted block of positions and gaps. Those positions, together with control of the remaining zeros, feed the equations for backward gap motion. Enlarging \(K(T)\) makes that input more extensive. Joining it to a high-tail description and carrying the resulting gap control farther backward are further mathematical tasks.

I saved this explanation in [brainstorm Note 09](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/05_arithmetic_gap_continuation/03_explicit_zero_gap_transport/brainstorm/notes/09_EZ_TWO_LIMITS_AND_THE_ROLE_OF_K_20261120.md).

Some questions / comments:

- I'm confused by the discussion about the source resembling a mound around a. The formula written is an oscillatory function centered at x=0, not x=a, and a only comes in as a multiplicative constant in the phase. This doesn't align with the description of it being a mound centered at a.
I’ll check the notation and clarify the distinction between the source variable \(u\) and the height variable \(x\).

You’re right about the displayed formula: **its envelope is centered at \(x=0\)**. The “mound near \(a\)” refers to a different function, in the variable \(u\). I did not make that distinction clear.

There are two separate graphs:

| Object | Horizontal axis | Description |
|---|---|---|
| Source density \(\rho_T(u)\) | \(u\) | At large heat time, concentrated near \(u=a\) |
| Normalized field \(H_T(x)/H_T(0)\) | \(x\) | Oscillates approximately like a damped \(\cos(ax)\) |

The source density is
\[
\rho_T(u)=\frac{e^{Tu^2}\Phi(u)}{H_T(0)},\qquad u\ge0.
\]
The field is obtained by **transforming** that density:
\[
\frac{H_T(x)}{H_T(0)}
=\int_0^\infty \rho_T(u)\cos(xu)\,du.
\]
Thus the source and field are not the same curve with renamed variables.

An ideal Gaussian makes the relationship explicit. For this illustration, take a Gaussian on the whole \(u\)-line:
\[
\underbrace{\rho_G(u)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma}
 e^{-(u-a)^2/(2\sigma^2)}}_{\text{mound centered at }u=a}.
\]
Its cosine transform is exactly
\[
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\rho_G(u)\cos(xu)\,du
=
\underbrace{e^{-\sigma^2x^2/2}}_{\text{envelope centered at }x=0}
\underbrace{\cos(ax)}_{\text{oscillation frequency set by }a}.
\]

**The location of the mound becomes the frequency of the oscillation.** That is why \(a\) appears multiplicatively in the phase.

You can see this directly by writing \(u=a+v\):
\[
e^{ixu}=e^{iax}e^{ixv}.
\]
The displacement \(a\) in the source variable produces a phase factor \(e^{iax}\) in the transformed variable. For a symmetric Gaussian, the remaining centered transform is the positive envelope above.

So my earlier description should have said: **the heated source is concentrated near \(u=a\); its transform, viewed as a function of height \(x\), resembles a damped cosine with frequency \(a\).** Also, \(a\) is precisely the source’s mean; its actual maximum need not sit exactly there.

I’ve clarified this in [Note 09](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/05_arithmetic_gap_continuation/03_explicit_zero_gap_transport/brainstorm/notes/09_EZ_TWO_LIMITS_AND_THE_ROLE_OF_K_20261120.md).

Ok so it sounds like there are two separate approximations here. One of them works better at large height for fixed time, and the other one works better for smaller height? Can you explain the large height approximation more? The explanation referencing A_t(x) is short and hand wavy.
I’ll unpack the large-height formula: what its amplitude and phase are, why the error shrinks with height, and how that locates the zeros.

The mechanism is more concrete than the notation \(A_t(x)\) suggested. The formula has two conjugate oscillatory sums. At positive heat time, increasing height suppresses every term after the first in each sum. Those two surviving terms produce the cosine, with a phase determined explicitly by the gamma factor.

The explicit phase shows why the high zeros get closer together: it advances at roughly \(\tfrac14\log(x/(4\pi))\), so one half-turn takes about \(4\pi/\log x\) units of height. The remainder also shrinks relative to the wave’s amplitude, which makes the position error shrink even as a fraction of that spacing.

Yes—with one qualification: **our inverse approximation works from the origin through a growing range when heat time is large.** Small height alone does not justify it at arbitrary time.

For the large-height approximation, we can replace the unexplained \(A_t(x)\) with explicit formulas. I’ll use fixed \(0<t\le \tfrac12\), the range of the published estimates.

Put
\[
\ell_x=\log\frac{x}{4\pi}.
\]
Define the positive envelope
\[
\mathcal A_t(x)=
\frac{\pi^{1/4}}{16}x^{7/4}
\exp\!\left(
-\frac{\pi x}{8}
+\frac{t\ell_x^2}{16}
-\frac{t\pi^2}{64}
\right)
\]
and the phase
\[
\varphi_t(x)=
\frac{x}{4}(\ell_x-1)
+\frac{7\pi}{8}
+\frac{t\pi}{16}\ell_x.
\]
Expanding the published model gives
\[
\boxed{
H_t(x)=\mathcal A_t(x)
\left[\cos\varphi_t(x)+O(x^{-ct})\right]
}
\]
for sufficiently large \(x\), with some constant \(c>0\). Everything in the envelope and phase is explicitly determined by \(t\) and \(x\). The error is measured relative to the envelope, including near the zeros. [Polymath, Proposition 9.1 and Lemma 9.2](https://arxiv.org/html/1904.12438v2#S9)

The envelope tells us how large the oscillations are. The phase tells us where they cross zero. Since the envelope is positive, it does not move the predicted zeros.

**Where does this particular oscillation come from?**

At time zero, with \(s=(1+ix)/2\), we have
\[
H_0(x)=
\underbrace{\frac{s(s-1)}{16}\pi^{-s/2}\Gamma(s/2)}_{G(s)}
\,\zeta(s).
\]
The gamma factor has an explicitly calculable magnitude and phase at large height. Applying Stirling’s formula gives
\[
G\!\left(\frac{1+ix}{2}\right)
\approx
\frac{\pi^{1/4}}{32}x^{7/4}e^{-\pi x/8}
\exp\!\left[
i\left(\frac{x}{4}(\ell_x-1)+\frac{7\pi}{8}\right)
\right].
\]
Thus the basic decay and oscillation already come from the completion factor. The coefficients above follow by substituting \(s=(1+ix)/2\) into [complex Stirling’s formula](https://dlmf.nist.gov/5.11.E1).

The arithmetic part supplies additional oscillations. A Riemann–Siegel representation organizes the full field into two conjugate sums indexed by integers \(n\), plus a controlled remainder. After heating, the first term of each sum gives a complex quantity \(P_t(x)\) and its conjugate:
\[
P_t(x)+\overline{P_t(x)}
=2|P_t(x)|\cos(\arg P_t(x)).
\]
This is the origin of the cosine. Heating modifies the gamma-derived amplitude and phase by the explicit \(t\)-dependent terms displayed above.

But that leaves the decisive question: **why are we allowed to discard the terms with \(n\ge2\)?**

Here is the actual suppression mechanism. After extracting the common amplitude, the \(n\)-th term has, to leading order, magnitude
\[
w_n(t,x)\approx
\frac1{\sqrt n}
\exp\!\left[
-\frac t4\log n\,(\ell_x-\log n)
\right].
\]

For \(n=1\), this weight is exactly \(1\). For each fixed \(n\ge2\), it decreases with height like
\[
\text{constant depending on }t,n
\;\times\;x^{-\,t\log n/4}.
\]
So increasing height suppresses the later arithmetic terms **relative to the first term**.

This also works for the whole growing sum, not just each fixed \(n\). Its cutoff is approximately \(n\le\sqrt{x/(4\pi)}\), so \(\log n\le\ell_x/2\). Consequently the weights are bounded, up to small corrections, by
\[
w_n(t,x)\lesssim n^{-1/2-t\ell_x/8}.
\]
The exponent grows without bound when \(t>0\) is fixed. Hence the combined contribution from all \(n\ge2\) tends to zero. The algebra follows from the heat weights and shifted exponent in [Polymath’s equations (15), (17), and (21)](https://arxiv.org/html/1904.12438v2#S1).

That is the concrete reason the field approaches a single explicit cosine: **the arithmetic corrections to the two leading conjugate terms become progressively smaller.**

**How does this become an approximation for individual zeros?**

Predict a zero at \(u\) by solving
\[
\varphi_t(u)=\left(m+\frac12\right)\pi.
\]
This is an elementary equation in \(u\). Near that crossing, a small displacement \(\delta\) changes the cosine by approximately
\[
\pm\varphi_t'(u)\delta,
\qquad
\varphi_t'(u)=
\frac14\log\frac{u}{4\pi}+\frac{t\pi}{16u}.
\]
Therefore an error of size \(\varepsilon\) in cosine units corresponds to a position error of order
\[
\frac{\varepsilon}{\varphi_t'(u)}.
\]

Taking \(\varepsilon=O(u^{-ct})\), the published localization and counting argument gives a unique nearby zero with
\[
|\text{actual zero}-u|
=O\!\left(\frac{u^{-ct}}{\log u}\right).
\]
Meanwhile, consecutive predicted zeros require a phase advance of \(\pi\), giving spacing approximately
\[
\frac{\pi}{\varphi_t'(u)}
\sim\frac{4\pi}{\log u}.
\]
Dividing these two quantities shows that the position error **as a fraction of the spacing** tends to zero. [Polymath, proof following (104)](https://arxiv.org/html/1904.12438v2#S9)

There is a crucial time dependence here. At \(t=0\), the suppression factor disappears: the weights above revert to \(n^{-1/2}\). The sufficient high-height threshold behaves like \(e^{C/t}\), so it recedes to infinity as time approaches zero. This is why increasingly accurate high-zero formulas at each fixed positive time do not automatically settle what happens at time zero.

Oh bummer I think RH has already been proved [https://www.washingtonpost.com/technology/2026/11/20/using-anthropic-ai-mathematician-claims-have-solved-riemann-hypothesis/](https://www.washingtonpost.com/technology/2026/11/20/using-anthropic-ai-mathematician-claims-have-solved-riemann-hypothesis/) at least that's the claim
I’ll check the article and look for the claimed proof and any independent mathematical assessment.

There is a public Lean formalization behind the announcement. The independent checking project I found reports that its preliminary checks passed, while the full proof check is still in progress. I’m checking the discussion Tao points to for any newer result.

I understand why that feels deflating. **There is a substantial public submission behind the headline, but the verification I could inspect is still unfinished.**

Levent Alpöge has released a large Lean formalization claiming RH and the generalized Riemann hypothesis for **Dirichlet \(L\)-functions**. The public release includes a theorem stated using Mathlib’s standard definition of RH. [Public source mirror](https://github.com/CocoSgt/riemann-hypothesis-lean)

An independent checking project reports preliminary checks of the source, statements, and dependencies. Its latest published status still says the full build is in progress; it has not posted a completed verification of the claimed proof. [Verification notes](https://github.com/Deicyde/riemann-hypothesis/blob/main/verification/NOTES.md)

Tao also discusses the announcement today and points to ongoing efforts to verify the formalization and understand its mathematical strategy. That is evidence that this deserves serious attention, rather than certification that the checking has finished. [Tao’s discussion](https://terrytao.wordpress.com/2026/11/20/unforced-euler-singularity-unforced-navier-stokes-singularity-and-the-generalized-riemann-hypothesis/)

So I would currently describe it as **a public, formally stated claimed proof undergoing independent verification**. A successful independent check would be decisive mathematical evidence even before people had distilled a readable explanation. I haven’t checked the proof myself.

For our program, we should be candid: **if this is validated, RH itself—and any established RH-equivalent positivity target—would already be settled.** That changes the purpose of pursuing those targets. But RH’s statement alone does not supply explicit zero locations, quantitative gap estimates, or an explanation of their motion under heat deformation. Those questions can retain independent content; we would need to compare the actual argument with our work before judging novelty.

I would take this announcement seriously and understand what it proves before investing substantially more effort in an independent route to RH.
